steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a blockchain security paper proposing private, anonymous, collateralizable commitments as a defence against MEV. Explain the MEV problem and why existing privacy approaches fall short, then describe our contribution, and finish with an organization-of-the-paper subsection.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- MEV
  - Miner-/maximal-extractable value (MEV) losses on Ethereum upwards of \$500M (cite); all blockchains likely billions
  - incurred by protocol users; diverts funds to extractors (only interested in extraction techniques); deters prospective users
  - cause: users announce intent (unencrypted transaction in mempool) before on-chain execution
  - two primary sources: decentralized exchange (DEX), auctions (liquidation, non-fungible token auctions, etc.)
  - intent reveals order price, order size, sender identity, trading history, account balances -> extraction

- Existing approaches
  - protocols hiding some of this information (cite); no satisfactory decentralized solution
  - zero-knowledge mixers, as used in (cite): join anonymity set, send/commit to send by revealing only set membership
  - must join anonymity sets in advance; need many other players to hide identity
  - disjoint anonymity sets (all listed protocols) -> tokens restricted to one protocol in advance
  - on-/off-boarding costly on-chain (merkle-tree additions, proof-verification) -> bottlenecks

## I-A Our Contribution

- address limits of single-use anonymity sets, costly waiting times for collateral
- improved variant of single-use collateralized commitments, as used in (cite)
  - dynamic: collateral locked instantaneously; commitments for almost any transaction
  - private (nothing about the purpose leaked), anonymous (no way to learn the initiating user)
- immediate consequences for MEV in DEXs, auctions, and beyond

- PACCs
  - Private, Anonymous, Collateralizable Commitments: based on smart contract wallets (SCWs) and Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs)
  - convinces block builder/relayer: enough funds for fees; wallet committed to actions; collateral lost if broken
  - expensive operations off-chain (ZKPs); few extra mapping checks vs. externally owned accounts (EOA), as in Ethereum (cite)
  - mappings: gas-efficient storage structures; used to enforce commitments

- Properties and implementation
  - properties (Section VI); effectively eliminate MEV in DEXs, liquidations, auctions
  - MEV shifted to censorship, still a concern; arbitrarily expensive (cite): accept commitments long enough (parameter \Delta, Section IV), transactions practically indistinguishable
  - proof-of-concept: gas consumption, computing times; feasibility

## I-B Organization of the Paper

- II: previous work on information hiding for MEV-protection
- III: cryptographic primitives
- IV: PACC protocol; V: proof-of-concept and benchmarks
- VI: general properties; VI-A: MEV protection in decentralized finance
- VII: conclusion and further discussion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Miner-/maximal-extractable value (MEV) losses on Ethereum are more than \$500M, and the actual losses across all blockchains are likely in the billions. Protocol users are the ones incurring these losses. If genuine protocol users lose money, funds are diverted away from protocols to extractors, entities only interested in investing in extraction techniques, and it is also a clear deterrent for prospective users. This happens as a direct consequence of users announcing an intent to do something (adding an unencrypted transaction to the mempool) before the action is executed on-chain. In the two main sources of MEV, decentralized exchange (DEX) and auctions (liquidation auctions, non-fungible token auctions, etc.), this intent usually reveals some combination of order price, order size, sender identity, trading history, and account balances. All this information lets extractors extract value from players in a blockchain.

Some protocols have emerged in the literature to hide some of this information, but no satisfactory decentralized solution has been found. One emergent technology that hides transaction information effectively on public blockchains is zero-knowledge mixers, as used in some of these protocols. With these, players join an anonymity set and send/commit to send transactions by revealing (only) membership in a set. Unfortunately existing solutions require players to join anonymity sets before proving membership, and they need many other players to join the set to hide identity adequately. If protocols have disjoint anonymity sets, which is the case for all of the listed protocols, then a player has to restrict tokens to one of these protocols before using the tokens. Also, on-boarding and off-boarding into these anonymity sets need costly on-chain operations (merkle-tree additions, proof-verification), and these are bottlenecks for prospective protocols based on these anonymity sets.

## I-A Our Contribution

In this paper we address the limitations of single-use anonymity sets and their waiting times for collateral to be usable, which can be costly. We propose an improved variant of single-use collateralized commitments, as used in existing systems, with a dynamic variation where collateral can be locked instantly for its required purpose, and where commitments are possible for almost any transaction, while the transaction is effectively kept private (no information about what the transaction itself is for is leaked) and anonymous (there is no way to learn who the user initiating the transaction is). These improvements are crucial and have immediate consequences for MEV, minimizing MEV opportunities as they currently occur in DEXs, auctions, and beyond.

- PACCs
  - Private, Anonymous, Collateralizable Commitments: based on smart contract wallets (SCWs) and Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs)
  - convinces block builder/relayer: enough funds for fees; wallet committed to actions; collateral lost if broken
  - expensive operations off-chain (ZKPs); few extra mapping checks vs. externally owned accounts (EOA), as in Ethereum (cite)
  - mappings: gas-efficient storage structures; used to enforce commitments

- Properties and implementation
  - properties (Section VI); effectively eliminate MEV in DEXs, liquidations, auctions
  - MEV shifted to censorship, still a concern; arbitrarily expensive (cite): accept commitments long enough (parameter \Delta, Section IV), transactions practically indistinguishable
  - proof-of-concept: gas consumption, computing times; feasibility

## I-B Organization of the Paper

- II: previous work on information hiding for MEV-protection
- III: cryptographic primitives
- IV: PACC protocol; V: proof-of-concept and benchmarks
- VI: general properties; VI-A: MEV protection in decentralized finance
- VII: conclusion and further discussion

steps.text:
Miner-/maximal-extractable value (MEV) losses on Ethereum are more than \$500M, and the actual losses across all blockchains are likely in the billions. Protocol users are the ones incurring these losses. If genuine protocol users lose money, funds are diverted away from protocols to extractors, entities only interested in investing in extraction techniques, and it is also a clear deterrent for prospective users. This happens as a direct consequence of users announcing an intent to do something (adding an unencrypted transaction to the mempool) before the action is executed on-chain. In the two main sources of MEV, decentralized exchange (DEX) and auctions (liquidation auctions, non-fungible token auctions, etc.), this intent usually reveals some combination of order price, order size, sender identity, trading history, and account balances. All this information lets extractors extract value from players in a blockchain.

Some protocols have emerged in the literature to hide some of this information, but no satisfactory decentralized solution has been found. One emergent technology that hides transaction information effectively on public blockchains is zero-knowledge mixers, as used in some of these protocols. With these, players join an anonymity set and send/commit to send transactions by revealing (only) membership in a set. Unfortunately existing solutions require players to join anonymity sets before proving membership, and they need many other players to join the set to hide identity adequately. If protocols have disjoint anonymity sets, which is the case for all of the listed protocols, then a player has to restrict tokens to one of these protocols before using the tokens. Also, on-boarding and off-boarding into these anonymity sets need costly on-chain operations (merkle-tree additions, proof-verification), and these are bottlenecks for prospective protocols based on these anonymity sets.

## I-A Our Contribution

In this paper we address the limitations of single-use anonymity sets and their waiting times for collateral to be usable, which can be costly. We propose an improved variant of single-use collateralized commitments, as used in existing systems, with a dynamic variation where collateral can be locked instantly for its required purpose, and where commitments are possible for almost any transaction, while the transaction is effectively kept private (no information about what the transaction itself is for is leaked) and anonymous (there is no way to learn who the user initiating the transaction is). These improvements are crucial and have immediate consequences for MEV, minimizing MEV opportunities as they currently occur in DEXs, auctions, and beyond.

We describe Private, Anonymous, Collateralizable Commitments (PACCs), which is a commitment protocol based on smart contract wallets (SCWs) and Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs). With PACCs a prospective block builder or relayer can be convinced that the user generating the PACC has enough funds to pay the required fees, that its wallet is committed to performing certain actions, and, importantly, that the wallet will lose some amount of collateral if the commitment is broken. Our protocol does the expensive computing operations off-chain (i.e. computing ZKPs), and only needs a few additional mapping checks compared to transactions sent from basic externally owned accounts (EOA), as in Ethereum. Mappings are storage structures that are gas-efficient and implemented on smart contract-enabled blockchains, and in our construction we use them to enforce commitments.

We outline what the properties of PACCs are (Section VI), and we show how they can be applied to effectively eliminate MEV as it is known in DEXs, liquidations and auctions. PACCs shift MEV to censorship, and censorship is still a concern. But we believe censorship can be made arbitrarily expensive by forcing protocols to accept commitments for long enough (in the model assumption of Section IV we introduce a parameter \Delta for this long enough), and by making all transactions practically indistinguishable, which PACCs achieves.

We also implement a proof-of-concept of PACCs, which lets us gather information about our solution (e.g. smart contract gas consumption, computing times), and it proves that it is feasible.

## I-B Organization of the Paper

In Section II we analyze previous work on information hiding in the context of MEV-protection. Section III introduces the cryptographic primitives that we need to reason formally about PACCs. In Section IV we define the PACC protocol, and Section V explains the proof-of-concept we implemented and the benchmarks we performed. Section VI outlines some general properties of PACCs. Section VI-A shows the potential of PACCs for protecting against MEV, specifically for decentralized finance. We conclude in Section VII with some further discussion on PACCs.

It is a direct consequence of users announcing an intent to do something (adding an unencrypted transaction to the mempool) before that action is executed on-chain. In the two primary sources of MEV, decentralized exchange (DEX) and auctions (liquidation auctions, non-fungible token auctions, etc.), this intent typically reveals some combination of order price, order size, sender identity, trading history, and account balances. All of this information allows extractors to extract value from players in a blockchain.

Although some protocols have emerged in the literature to hide some of this information [3,4,5,6,7,8,9], no satisfactory decentralized solution has been found. Furthermore, on-boarding and off-boarding into these anonymity sets require costly on-chain operations (merkle-tree additions, proof-verification), which serve as bottlenecks to prospective protocols based on these anonymity sets.

## I-A Our Contribution

In this paper, we address the limitations of single-use anonymity sets and their potentially costly waiting times for collateral to be usable. PACCs can be used to convince a prospective block builder or relayer that the user generating the PACC has enough funds to pay the required fees, that its wallet is committed to performing certain actions, and, importantly, that the wallet loses some amount of collateral if this commitment is broken. Furthermore, we implement a proof-of-concept of PACCs that allows us to gather information about our solution (e.g. smart contract gas consumption, computing times) and proves its feasibility.

Section II analyzes previous work related to information hiding in the context of MEV-protection. Section III introduces the cryptographic primitives needed to reason formally about PACCs. Section IV defines the PACC protocol, and Section V explains the proof-of-concept we implemented, along with the benchmarks we performed. Some general properties of PACCs are outlined in Section VI, and Section VI-A demonstrates the potential of PACCs in protecting against MEV, specifically in decentralized finance.
